issues.legal_issue: The intent to annoy required for criminal trespass is established when the circumstances show that causing annoyance was the aim of the entry, rather than merely a likely consequence.
material_facts: The complainant obtained actual physical possession of the land after prolonged litigation and the respondents' resistance to execution of the ejectment decree.
About two weeks after possession was delivered, the respondents entered the land and were found preparing to construct bamboo structures.
The court found no other dominant intention that could explain the respondents' entry.
issues.conclusion: The respondents' intention was to annoy the complainant, and the intent required for criminal trespass was established.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 441 and 447 of the Indian Penal Code, causing annoyance must be the aim of the entry; it is not enough that annoyance was merely a likely natural consequence known to the entrant. The court must consider all relevant circumstances, including such knowledge and the probability of another dominant intention. The court applied Mathuri and Others v. State of Punjab, [1964] 5 S.C.R. 916, 927.

rule.if: criminal_trespass_prosecution and prior_possession_recovered_after_dispute and entry_followed_by_construction_preparations and no_other_dominant_purpose

predicates.criminal_trespass_prosecution: The proceeding concerns an alleged entry onto property with the intent required for criminal trespass.
predicates.prior_possession_recovered_after_dispute: The complainant recovered possession of the property after a dispute with the entrants.
predicates.entry_followed_by_construction_preparati: The entrants entered the property and then prepared to construct structures there.
predicates.no_other_dominant_purpose: The circumstances disclose no other dominant purpose that prompted the entry.

issues.definition: When a criminal trespass prosecution involves recovered possession, entry followed by preparations to build, and no other dominant purpose, the rule treats the intent to annoy as established.

issues.legal_issue: A person who has obtained possession of vacant land may remain in actual possession while the land is unoccupied.
material_facts: The complainant obtained actual physical possession of the land through execution of an ejectment decree.
The land remained vacant after possession was delivered to the complainant and until the respondents entered it.
issues.conclusion: The complainant was in actual possession of the vacant land after obtaining possession of it.
issues.legal_principle: For the purposes of sections 441 and 447 of the Indian Penal Code, vacant land may be in the actual possession of the person to whom possession has been delivered even though that person is not physically occupying it. The court's determination is consistent with its application of Mathuri and Others v. State of Punjab, [1964] 5 S.C.R. 916, 927, on assessing the circumstances of an alleged trespass.

predicates.criminal_trespass_prosecution: The proceeding concerns an alleged entry onto property with the intent required for criminal trespass.
predicates.possession_delivered_to_complainant: The complainant received physical possession of the land.
predicates.land_remained_vacant: The land was unoccupied after possession was delivered and before the alleged entry.

issues.definition: When a complainant receives possession of land that remains vacant, the rule treats the complainant as being in actual possession.

issues.legal_issue: The person intended to be annoyed by an entry onto property need not be physically present when the entry occurs.
material_facts: The complainant had obtained possession of the land before the respondents entered it.
The High Court treated the complainant's absence at the time of entry as a bar to criminal trespass, but the Supreme Court rejected that requirement.
issues.conclusion: The law does not require the person intended to be annoyed to be present at the time of the trespass.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 441 and 447 of the Indian Penal Code do not require the person whom the entrant intends to annoy to be physically present at the time of entry. The court applied the principles in Mathuri and Others v. State of Punjab, [1964] 5 S.C.R. 916, 927, under which intent is assessed from the aim of the entry and all relevant circumstances.

predicates.criminal_trespass_prosecution: The proceeding concerns an alleged entry onto property with the intent required for criminal trespass.
predicates.intended_target_absent_at_entry: The person whom the entrant allegedly intended to annoy was not physically present when the entry occurred.

issues.definition: When the intended target is absent during an entry alleged to be criminal trespass, the rule does not require that person's physical presence.
